facts.text: Writer Will Schmitz says he first conceived this story as "One Woman Death Machine", and that the finished film differs greatly from his draft. Director David DeCoteau's version won out.
Director David DeCoteau shot his previous film, Creepozoids (1987), in 15 days in a Los Angeles warehouse for about $150,000. He says it was his first feature shot on 35mm.

Director David DeCoteau fired actor William Butler during this shoot and wrote him out of the film. He told Draculina magazine Butler was "single handedly the most difficult actor I ever worked with."
Director David DeCoteau told Horrorfan in 1989, "Women are the aggressors in my movies." Lady Avenger and its fighting heroine, Maggie, fit that pattern.
Peggy McIntaggart, who plays Maggie, is billed as "Peggie Sanders" on some listings. She became Playboy's Playmate of the Month in January 1990, about two years after this film.
Before Hollywood, Peggy McIntaggart (Maggie) entered the 1980 Miss Nude World contest in Stoney Creek, Ontario "on a dare", and she won.
Michelle Bauer (Annalee) is billed here as "Michelle McClellan", her second husband's name. She used it the same year for Hollywood Chainsaw Hookers (1988), before switching back to Bauer.
The film's tagline was "You've seen the rest… now meet the best."
Director David DeCoteau says action was "the most commercially viable" genre overseas. That's why he made Lady Avenger and Ghetto Blaster, which he says "did very, very well."
Scream queen Linnea Quigley sent director David DeCoteau to Michelle Bauer. He had worked with Quigley on a short film, and she referred him to Bauer, who plays Annalee here.
In 2007, director David DeCoteau said he owned the rights to Lady Avenger, Ghetto Blaster and Murder Weapon. He was holding them until Code Red, a cult-DVD label, set up its new distribution.
In the UK, Palace Video's tape was cut by the BBFC (classified March 22, 1988). The cuts removed a rape sequence and about a minute and a half of other violence.
Matty Budrewicz of The Schlock Pit called Lady Avenger "a potent poverty row action caper and an effective domestic drama." He said star Peggy McIntaggart's key-art presence is no accident.

Producer Marco Colombo's Filmtrust backed this film. He went on to produce Ghetto Blaster (1989) and about twenty-six more films with director David DeCoteau, including Bigfoot vs. D.B. Cooper (2016).
Writer Will Schmitz also wrote an unused early version of Creepozoids (1987), which director David DeCoteau made the year before this film. Schmitz's draft was titled "Mutant Spawn 2000."
Director David DeCoteau began his career in 1980 as a production assistant at Roger Corman's New World Pictures. He has also been credited under pseudonyms like Ellen Cabot and Julian Breen.
Michelle Bauer (Annalee) landed her first B-movie lead in The Tomb (1986) after director Fred Olen Ray cast her on condition that she dye her hair black. She became a leading '80s scream queen.
After acting, Peggy McIntaggart (Maggie) became a pro makeup artist, hair stylist and photographer. She even worked as Hugh Hefner's makeup artist and hair stylist.
The Girls with Guns site gave Lady Avenger 2.5 out of 5. It called it "surprisingly semi-competent" and cheesy 1980s fun, best enjoyed with a few beers.
Red Letter Media picked Lady Avenger on its Best of the Worst series. In the "Blindfold Picks" episode, the hosts choose VHS tapes without seeing them.
Director David DeCoteau executive-produced J.R. Bookwalter's Robot Ninja (1989) after offering Bookwalter a $15,000 budget. The film was shot in Ohio, and Linnea Quigley is in the cast.
The film shot around Los Angeles, including the Anderson Street overpass in Downtown LA and Wilmington, plus Piru, California.
Lady Avenger got a shout-out in the 1989 B-movie Robot Ninja. It was also referenced in Invasion of the Scream Queens (1992).
The Schlock Pit notes the song "Savage Streets" was used in the 1985 film Club Life before this one. Singer Rainey Haynes is also known for performing it in Girls of Rock & Roll.
The end-credits song "Savage Streets" was performed by Rainey Haynes. She also sang it in Girls of Rock & Roll (1985), the first original Playboy Home Video production.
